Here are two four-bar arrangements. Each one states the motif in bars 1–2, then extends it to a cadence in bars 3–4. I've kept the left hand simple with half-note or quarter-note chords so the right hand can focus on the eighth-note melody.

---

## Version 1: A Minor (Melodic Minor Ascending, Natural Descending)

### Right Hand (treble clef, eighth notes)

**Bar 1:** C4 – E4 – F#4 – G#4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 2:** A4 – G4 – E4 – D4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 3:** C4 – E4 – G4 – A4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 4:** G4 – E4 – D4 – A3 (last note held as a quarter, giving a half-beat rest or fermata to breathe)

The ascending F# and G# in bar 1 give the melodic minor color. Bar 2 descends naturally (G natural, no sharps). Bar 3 restates the original arpeggiated shape, and bar 4 resolves down to A.

**RH Fingering (suggested):**
Bar 1: 1 – 3 – 4 – 5. Bar 2: 5 – 4 – 3 – 2. Bar 3: 1 – 3 – 4 – 5. Bar 4: 4 – 3 – 2 – 1.

### Left Hand (bass clef, half notes or quarter notes)

**Bar 1:** Am chord (A2 – C3 – E3), held as a half note, then D major (D2 – F#2 – A2) as a half note to support the F#.
**Bar 2:** E major (E2 – G#2 – B2) half note, then Am (A2 – C3 – E3) half note.
**Bar 3:** Am (A2 – C3 – E3) whole note, held through the bar.
**Bar 4:** E major (E2 – G#2 – B2) half note, then Am (A2 – C3 – E3) half note, final chord held or with fermata.

**LH Fingering:**
For Am (A2–C3–E3): 5 – 3 – 1. For D major (D2–F#2–A2): 5 – 3 – 1. For E major (E2–G#2–B2): 5 – 3 – 1.

### Dynamics and Articulation
Start mezzo-piano. Play the eighth notes legato, connecting each note smoothly. In bar 1, let the line grow slightly (small crescendo) as it rises through F# and G#. Bar 2 relaxes dynamically as you descend. Bar 4's final A can be played a touch softer, piano, to feel like settling. The left-hand chords should stay quieter than the melody throughout.

---

## Version 2: C Minor (Harmonic Minor)

### Right Hand (treble clef, eighth notes)

**Bar 1:** C4 – Eb4 – G4 – Ab4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 2:** G4 – Eb4 – D4 – C4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 3:** C4 – Eb4 – G4 – Ab4 (four eighth notes)
**Bar 4:** G4 – F4 – D4 – B3 – C4 (the first four as eighth notes, final C4 as a quarter note to end)

Bar 4 introduces the B natural (harmonic minor leading tone) on the last eighth note before resolving up to C. This gives a strong sense of arrival.

**RH Fingering:**
Bar 1: 1 – 2 – 4 – 5. Bar 2: 4 – 3 – 2 – 1. Bar 3: 1 – 2 – 4 – 5. Bar 4: 4 – 3 – 2 – 1 – 1 (thumb shifts to C4 for the final note).

### Left Hand (bass clef, half notes)

**Bar 1:** Cm (C2 – Eb2 – G2) whole note.
**Bar 2:** Ab major (Ab2 – C3 – Eb3) half note, then Eb major (Eb2 – G2 – Bb2) half note.
**Bar 3:** Fm (F2 – Ab2 – C3) half note, then Cm (C2 – Eb2 – G2) half note.
**Bar 4:** G major (G2 – B2 – D3) half note, then Cm (C2 – Eb2 – G2) half note with fermata.

The G major chord in bar 4 contains the B natural, which doubles the leading tone in the right hand and creates the dominant-to-tonic resolution (V–i).

**LH Fingering:**
Cm (C2–Eb2–G2): 5 – 3 – 1. Ab major (Ab2–C3–Eb3): 5 – 3 – 1. Fm (F2–Ab2–C3): 5 – 3 – 1. G major (G2–B2–D3): 5 – 3 – 1.

### Dynamics and Articulation
Start mezzo-forte — C minor has a darker, fuller character, so a slightly stronger opening feels right. Keep eighth notes legato. In bar 4, make a slight ritardando (slow down) on the last two beats as the B natural resolves to C. The final Cm chord can be held with the pedal for resonance. Sustain pedal can also be used lightly at chord changes throughout, lifting and re-pressing with each new left-hand chord to keep the sound clean.

---

## General Practice Notes

Play hands separately first at a slow tempo (around 60–70 bpm, one beat per quarter note). Once each hand is comfortable, combine them. Listen for the left hand staying softer than the right so the melody sings. The A minor version has a gentler, more lyrical quality; the C minor version sounds darker and more dramatic — try both and see which suits the mood you're after.

turns.text:
## Tweaked Left-Hand Patterns

### A Minor — Alberti Bass (Low–High–Middle–High, eighth notes)

**Bar 1:** A2 – E3 – C3 – E3 | A2 – E3 – C3 – E3 (eight eighth notes total)
**Bar 2:** E2 – B2 – G#2 – B2 | A2 – E3 – C3 – E3
**Bar 3:** A2 – E3 – C3 – E3 | A2 – E3 – C3 – E3
**Bar 4:** E2 – B2 – G#2 – B2 | A2 – E3 – C3 – E3

LH fingering for the Alberti pattern: 5 – 1 – 3 – 1 throughout. The hand stays in one position per chord, so there is no jumping.

### C Minor — Broken Fifth (root–fifth alternating, quarter notes)

**Bar 1:** C2 – G2 – C2 – G2
**Bar 2:** Ab1 – Eb2 – Eb2 – Bb2
**Bar 3:** F2 – C3 – C2 – G2
**Bar 4:** G2 – D3 – C2 – G2

LH fingering: 5 – 1 for each pair. The hand shifts at each new chord but the interval is always a fifth, which is easy to find by feel.

### Alternative RH Fingering (Easier Spots)

In the A minor version bar 4, the original fingering 4–3–2–1 ending on low A3 can be awkward. Try instead: 5–3–2–1, which gives the pinky more room on G4 and lets the thumb land naturally on A3.

In the C minor version bar 4, the five-note bar (G4–F4–D4–B3–C4) is the trickiest moment. Instead of 4–3–2–1–1 with a thumb shift, try 4–3–2–1–2, crossing the index finger over the thumb to C4. Alternatively, simplify the bar to four notes: G4–D4–B3–C4 (fingering 4–3–2–1), which skips the F4 passing tone and still gives a clean cadence.

---

## Tempo, Pedal, and Performance Notes

**Metronome:** quarter note = 66–72 bpm to start. Once comfortable, 80–88 bpm feels musical without rushing. The A minor version can sit a touch slower (66–76) for its lyrical quality; the C minor version can push slightly faster (72–88) for energy.

**Pedal:** In the A minor Alberti version, use no pedal or very light pedal, changing with each chord (lift and re-press on beat 1 of each new harmony). The Alberti pattern provides its own sustain. In the C minor broken-fifth version, use pedal more freely: press on beat 1 of each bar, lift briefly on beat 3 or when the chord changes, and re-press. In bar 4, hold the pedal through the final Cm chord for resonance.

---

## LilyPond Source

Paste everything below into a file ending in `.ly` and compile with LilyPond (version 2.24 or later) to get a single-page PDF. Both pieces appear on one page as two separate scores.

```lilypond
\version "2.24.0"
\header {
  title = "Motif in A Minor and C Minor"
  subtitle = "Two 4-bar arrangements for piano"
  composer = "arr. for practice"
}

\paper {
  #(set-paper-size "letter")
  top-margin = 15
  bottom-margin = 15
  left-margin = 20
  right-margin = 20
}

% ---- A MINOR (melodic minor, Alberti LH) ----

rhAminor = \relative c' {
  \clef treble
  \key a \minor
  \time 4/4
  \tempo "Lyrical" 4 = 69
  \dynamicUp

  % Bar 1
  c8\mp\<( e fis gis
  % Bar 2
  a\mf\> g e d
  % Bar 3
  c\mp\< e g a
  % Bar 4
  g\mf\> e d a)\p\fermata r4
}

lhAminor = \relative c, {
  \clef bass
  \key a \minor
  \time 4/4

  % Bar 1 - Am Alberti
  a8\p e' c e  a, e' c e |
  % Bar 2 - E major then Am
  e, b' gis b  a e' c e |
  % Bar 3 - Am
  a, e' c e  a, e' c e |
  % Bar 4 - E major then Am
  e, b' gis b  a4\fermata r |
}

\score {
  \header {
    piece = "A Minor — Melodic Minor with Alberti Bass"
  }
  \new PianoStaff <<
    \new Staff = "right" \rhAminor
    \new Staff = "left" \lhAminor
  >>
  \layout { }
  \midi { }
}

% ---- C MINOR (harmonic minor, broken-fifth LH) ----

rhCminor = \relative c' {
  \clef treble
  \key c \minor
  \time 4/4
  \tempo "Darkly" 4 = 76

  % Bar 1
  c8\mf( ees g aes
  % Bar 2
  g ees d c
  % Bar 3
  c ees g aes
  % Bar 4
  g d b4) c4.\p\fermata r8
}

lhCminor = \relative c, {
  \clef bass
  \key c \minor
  \time 4/4

  % Bar 1 - C-G
  c4\mp g' c, g' |
  % Bar 2 - Ab-Eb, Eb-Bb
  aes, ees' ees bes' |
  % Bar 3 - F-C, C-G
  f, c' c, g' |
  % Bar 4 - G-D, C-G
  g d' c,4.\fermata r8 |
}

\score {
  \header {
    piece = "C Minor — Harmonic Minor with Broken Fifths"
  }
  \new PianoStaff <<
    \new Staff = "right" \rhCminor
    \new Staff = "left" \lhCminor
  >>
  \layout { }
  \midi { }
}
```

A few notes on the code: the `\midi { }` block inside each `\score` means LilyPond will also generate a MIDI file for each piece when you compile, so you can listen to it directly. The tempo markings in the code match the BPM suggestions above. If your LilyPond version differs slightly, the main thing to check is the `\version` line at the top — change it to match your installed version if needed.
